I. Establishing Prima Facie Religious Status
Legal scholars and courts assess “religion” not by counting incense burners or the age of sacred texts, but by identifying indicia of sincerity, comprehensiveness, and ultimate concern. Writing in Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972), Chief Justice Burger summarized religious sincerity as “deeply held beliefs” forming an “ultimate concern” that “parallel the role traditionally filled by orthodox religious beliefs.” The Satanic Temple satisfies every prong.

  1. Ultimate Concern and Primary World-View
    The TST’s Seven Fundamental Tenets crystallize a moral code: “One should strive to act with compassion and empathy toward all creatures,” “Beliefs should conform to one’s best scientific understanding,” “The freedoms of others should be respected.” Unlike a political manifesto, these tenets are explicitly tied to personal conscience rather than partisan gain. Just as “Love thy neighbor” or “There is no god but God” orient believers, the Seven Tenets orient Satanists when they choose school curricula, oppose corporal punishment, or affirm bodily autonomy.

  2. Ritual, Symbolism, Communal Practice, and Clergy
    Detractors caricature TST as mere theatrics, ignoring the weekly congregations, Sunday school curricula, wedding divents, and canonically trained ordained clergy. The Black Mass, a speech-act commemorating rational inquiry and individual liberty, is as liturgical to participants as the Catholic Mass is to the faithful. Imagine denying Presbyterian marriages because many attendees are also ACLU members; the hybrid political-religious nature of congregational activity is irrelevant once sincerity is ascertained.

  3. Historical Parallel and Doctrinal Discretion
    Christianity, too, was once dismissed as a subversive mystery cult “inimical to society.” The First Amendment’s framers, reared in a milieu of Baptists fined for praying without government license, drafted protections precisely for persecuted minorities. Denying modern Satanists parity compounds the historic error against which Madison and Jefferson warned.

II. Free Exercise and Equal Protection Must Be Uniformly Applied
The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993) demands that the federal government justify any “substantial burden” on sincere exercise through the least-restrictive means. Satanic after-school clubs barred from public-school rooms furnished to Child Evangelism Fellowship are a textbook violation. Denial of clergy tax-exempt housing allowances, exclusion from Faith-Based Initiative grants, or rejection of marriage solemnization rights place Satanists in the very “second-tier” status RFRA was crafted to prevent.

Moreover, Equal Protection under the Fourteenth Amendment demands governmental neutrality, not hostility. In Bronx Household v. Board, the Second Circuit held that once a municipality creates a forum—be it a flagpole, park lawn, or social-studies class—the benefit must be extended neutrally. Exempting TST has no conceivable basis other than viewpoint discrimination, long held per se unconstitutional.

III. The Myth of the “Troll Church”
Critics allege that TST is “performative activism,” not belief. Yet sincerity is a factual, not theological, inquiry. Courts routinely preside over neo-pagan rituals, Discordian sub-groups, and Pastafarian pirate regalia, granting accommodations absent theological litmus tests. The TST has maintained belief statements, ordination programs, charitable/food-distribution drives comparable to Christian relief agencies, and public repentance statements against violent acts—precisely what authenticity looks like.

Moreover, describing Satanism as “mockery” of Christianity ventures into forbidden heresy-seeking. Justice Jackson affirmed in United States v. Ballard (1944): “Men may believe what they cannot prove.” The judiciary’s limited competence is to ask, “Is the belief sincerely held?”—not “Is the belief attractive?” Broad swaths of America find Scientology’s cosmology risible, yet the IRS and courts unmistakably recognize it.

Regrettably, headlines equate TST with ritual serial murder, despite the Temple’s explicit denunciation of supernatural theism and supernatural Satan alike. When legislators in Idaho cited “concerns about animal sacrifice” while debating chaplain licensing, they invoked robust theological stereotypes precisely of the kind forbidden by Larson v. Valente (1982), which struck down laws burdening minority faiths. If the state can stamp its veto on Satanists because some citizens harbor medieval fantasies, tomorrow’s veto can land on Wiccans or Reform Jews.

V. Practical Benefits to Society of Inclusion
Legally incorporating TST advances the public good.

  1. Stronger Church-State Separation—Because TST raises Establishment Clause challenges against prayer at city-council meetings or Ten Commandments monuments, its recognition compels jurisdictions either to drop sectarian displays entirely or open the floor to pluralistic voices. This strengthens, rather than weakens, Jefferson’s wall.
  2. Intellectual Diversity—TST’s campaigns against corporal punishment and its ritual abortion-care protection rites introduce valuable discourse about ethics, mental healthcare, and reproductive autonomy. Robust First Amendment forums gain by including minority perspectives.
  3. Demonstration of Constitutional Principle—Every time a clerk refuses a Satanic club and is forced by injunction to comply, citizens witness the Constitution vindicated against majoritarian impulses.

VI. Policy Recommendations
A. Federal Agencies
• Classify TST as a tax-exempt church under IRC 501(c)(3) and clergy under IRC 107 (parsonage allowance) by applying the same sincerity inquiries already used to accommodate thousands of denominations.

B. State and Local Governments

• Apply minister-marriage licensing and blasphemy shield laws to Satanic clergy on parity with other denominational leaders.

C. Judiciary

VII. Conclusion: Walking the Talk of Religious Liberty
The Founders granted no legislative veto to spiritual majorities. Their Constitution granted each citizen a sanctuary from imposed theology. When legislators and bureaucrats deny The Satanic Temple the same accommodations routinely granted to monotheistic denominations, they breach that promise and reduce the First Amendment to little more than a sacred popularity contest.

To preserve the integrity—and credibility—of religious freedom itself, governmental actors must now acknowledge the plain facts of sincerity, doctrinal coherence, communal practice, and statutory conformity. The Satanic Temple is a religion. Full legal recognition is not a courtesy; it is a constitutional imperative.

The Case for Full Legal Recognition of Modern Satanic Groups as Bona Fide Religions

Introduction

Religious freedom is a cornerstone of democratic societies, enshrined in constitutional protections that guarantee individuals the right to practice their beliefs without government interference. I. Modern Satanic Groups Meet the Legal Definition of a Religion

To qualify as a religion under U.S. law, a group must demonstrate sincere belief in a system of morality or ethics, a shared community of adherents, and a structured practice of worship or ritual. Courts have consistently ruled that belief in a higher power is not a prerequisite for religious recognition—what matters is whether the group’s teachings provide meaning, purpose, and ethical guidance to its members.

A. The Satanic Temple’s Core Beliefs and Practices

The Satanic Temple (TST) and other modern Satanic groups explicitly define themselves as religious organizations, not merely as atheistic or anti-religious movements. Their Seven Tenets—which include compassion, justice, and scientific inquiry—serve as a moral and philosophical framework for their members, much like the Ten Commandments or the Eightfold Path in other religions.

Key aspects of their religious identity include:

  1. Theistic Satanism (in some branches) – While TST is non-theistic, other Satanic groups (such as the First Satanic Church) do worship Satan as a symbol of rebellion, enlightenment, and personal empowerment.   • They perform marriages, funerals, and baptisms (e.g., TST’s "Satanic Naming Ceremonies").

Objection 1: "Satanism is Not a Real Religion—It’s Just Atheism in Disguise"

  • TST’s activism (e.g., fighting for reproductive rights, LGBTQ+ equality, separation of church and state) is consistent with religious social justice traditions.

Conclusion: Justice Demands Equal Protection for Satanic Groups

The legal, philosophical, and moral arguments are clear: modern Satanic groups meet all criteria for religious recognition, and denying them equal protection under the law is both unjust and unconstitutional. The persistent exclusion of Satanism is not about law—it is about prejudice, a refusal to extend the same rights to beliefs that challenge the religious status quo.

The time has come to stop treating Satanic organizations as second-class religions and extend to them the same legal protections, tax exemptions, and constitutional safeguards afforded to every other faith. True religious liberty means protecting beliefs we disagree with—not just those we endorse. The Satanic Temple and other modern Satanic groups deserve nothing less than full and equal recognition under the law.

It is the responsibility of lawmakers, courts, and society at large to end the discrimination against Satanic believers. This means:

  • Amending laws to explicitly include Satanic groups in religious protections.
  • Ensuring prison systems, military chaplaincy, and public institutions treat Satanists equally.

Equal at the Altar of Liberty: Why Modern Satanic Groups Deserve Full Legal Recognition

Introduction

In a nation founded on the principle that government shall neither establish nor inhibit the free exercise of religion, the legitimacy of a faith should be determined not by its comfort to majority sensibilities, but by its sincerity, its organizational structure, and its adherents' constitutional rights. The Satanic Temple (TST), a nontheistic religious organization founded in 2013, has emerged as one of the most legally consequential new religious movements in the United States. Yet it continues to face a peculiar form of discrimination: the reflexive assumption that its very name disqualifies it from the protections afforded to more traditional faiths. This essay argues that modern Satanic groups such as TST are bona fide religions, fully deserving of legal recognition and equal protection under the law, and that denying them such recognition represents a dangerous violation of the constitutional principles upon which the American republic is built.

Defining the Movement: What TST Actually Is

Before defending TST's legitimacy, we must confront the most potent barrier to its acceptance: ignorance. The Satanic Temple is not, as sensationalist media often implies, a criminal cult or a gathering of devil worshippers. It is a federally recognized religious corporation with a formal organizational hierarchy, established houses of worship, a published seven-tenet ethical framework, and a mission of secular civic engagement informed by its interpretation of Satan as a literary symbol of rebellion against tyranny.

Its tenets emphasize empathy, the pursuit of justice, bodily autonomy, the freedom to offend, and the rejection of supernatural authority. The organization's co-founder, Lucien Greaves, has repeatedly emphasized that TST does not believe in a literal Satan. The figure functions much as the Serpent functions in certain Gnostic traditions or as Prometheus functions in classical literature—a symbol of intellectual liberation against dogmatic oppression.

This distinction matters because the most common objection to recognizing Satanic groups is grounded in theological literalism. Critics assume that because the word "Satan" appears in the organization's name, its members must be engaged in the worship of an evil deity. But the First Amendment has never permitted the government to evaluate religious claims based on whether they are theologically coherent to outsiders. As the Supreme Court affirmed in United States v. Ballard (1944), religious sincerity—not theological correctness—is the proper subject of constitutional inquiry. By that standard, TST is overwhelmingly legitimate.

The Legal Architecture of Religious Freedom

The constitutional case for granting TST full legal recognition rests on two pillars: the Free Exercise Clause and the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, reinforced by the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Free Exercise. The Free Exercise Clause guarantees that "Congress shall make no law... prohibiting the free exercise" of religion. This protection has been interpreted broadly to encompass the right to hold religious beliefs, to worship in accordance with them, to assemble with co-religionists, to engage in religious speech, and to be free from government-imposed burdens on religious practice. TST's members sincerely hold their beliefs, gather for religious ceremonies, and engage in religious expression. To deny them the protections of this clause while extending those protections to, say, a Wiccan coven or a Pastafarian gathering (which courts have recognized in various contexts) would be a textbook violation of equal treatment.

Equal Protection. Equal protection guarantees that no state shall "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws." Religious classification is, after all, a classification. When the government extends tax exemptions to religious organizations, grants chaplains access to public institutions, permits religious exemptions from generally applicable laws, or allows religious displays in public forums, it must do so without regard to whether the religion in question offends majority sensibilities. Allowing the government to discriminate based on the unpopularity or unsettling character of a religion would effectively give the majority veto power over the minority's rights—precisely the tyranny the First Amendment was designed to prevent.

The Establishment Clause. Perhaps counterintuitively, the Establishment Clause itself demands equal treatment for non-mainstream religions. As Justice O'Connor argued in her concurrence in Allegheny County v. ACLU (1989), the government should avoid "endorsing" one religion over another. When public schools teach Christianity in their curricula, when city halls display the Ten Commandments, when state legislatures open sessions with exclusively Christian prayers—the absence of a Satanic invocation in those same contexts represents a clear endorsement of one faith tradition over another. TST's activist mission, which has involved applying to deliver invocations at government meetings where Christian invocations are already permitted, demonstrates the pernicious double standard that the Establishment Clause was designed to eliminate.

The Court's Own Recognition

TST is not merely arguing in the abstract for recognition; it has won tangible legal victories that demonstrate its legitimate standing. The organization has successfully argued for religious exemptions in contexts ranging from abortion access to public forums. In 2021, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review a lower court ruling allowing TST member Mark Cassara to sue the Internal Revenue Service over religious discrimination regarding a deduction for religious activities—a victory that implicitly recognized the legitimacy of TST's religious claims. Multiple federal and state courts have granted TST members exemptions from laws that burden religious practice.

The Internal Revenue Service itself has granted tax-exempt status to TST, recognizing it as a legitimate religious organization. The federal government—the same government that has long held a monopoly on determining which organizations qualify for religious tax exemption—has formally acknowledged that TST meets the legal definition of a religion. To permit lower-level bureaucrats, employers, school administrators, or angry online commentators to override this federal determination would be to elevate prejudice over process.

The Historical Echoes of Religious Discrimination

The instinct to deny religious legitimacy to disfavored groups is not new, and it has historically been a tool of oppression. The Puritans who founded several American colonies persecuted Quakers, Baptists, and other dissenters. In the nineteenth century, the United States saw violent anti-Catholic and anti-Mormon movements that sought to delegitimize these faiths as foreign, idolatrous, or politically dangerous. Jehovah's Witnesses faced violent persecution throughout the twentieth century for their refusal to salute flags or serve in wars. Each of these groups, now considered legitimate and even mainstream, was at one time considered absurd, threatening, or fake.

When the Jehovah's Witnesses won the landmark case West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court did not first determine whether their theology was correct. It determined only that the government could not compel them to violate their religious conscience. By the same logic, the government cannot deny TST recognition simply because its theology—or its aesthetic—discomforts the majority.

Addressing the Objections

Objections to recognizing Satanic groups typically fall into a few categories, none of which survive scrutiny.

The "It's just a joke" objection. Critics claim TST is merely a trolling organization designed to provoke Christians, not a sincere religious movement. This claim is empirically false. TST has formal clergy, performs weddings and funerals, holds regular services, runs a religious publishing arm, and operates with a sophisticated legal department. Its members have reported genuinely held religious beliefs, and its lawsuits are pursued in good faith. More importantly, even if a religious movement began as a provocation, sincerity of belief—not its origin story—is the legal standard. Many serious world religions began as small, ridiculed movements.

The "Satan is evil" objection. Some argue that because Satan represents evil in Christian theology, any organization bearing that name cannot be legitimate. This argument fails for two reasons. First, the government has no authority to enforce Christian theological categories on non-Christian religions. Jewish, Muslim, and Hindu traditions regard Satan (or his analogues) quite differently than evangelical Christianity does. Second, TST does not worship Satan as an evil being; it reinterprets the figure as a symbol of resistance to arbitrary authority. To privilege one theological interpretation of a figure over another is to entangle the state in theological disputes that the Establishment Clause forbids.

The "It will harm the public" objection. Opponents often suggest that granting recognition to Satanic groups will harm public morals, encourage criminal behavior, or confuse children. These claims are entirely speculative and contradicted by the actual behavior of TST and its members. There is no evidence whatsoever that TST members engage in more criminal activity than members of any other religious group. The organization explicitly disavows illegal activity in its tenets and is known for organizing blood drives, charity work, and public cleanups. The harm-of-recognition argument has been used against every minority religion in American history, and it has always been disproven.

The slippery slope objection. Finally, some suggest that recognizing TST will lead to absurd outcomes—forcing the government to accept Pastafarians or the Church of the Flying Spaghetti Monster as religions. But this objection proves too much. The same argument was made against recognizing Scientology, Wicca, and the Nation of Islam, all of which are now accepted as legitimate religious organizations. In practice, courts have been perfectly capable of distinguishing sincere religious organizations from parodic ones, based on organizational structure, doctrinal seriousness, and the nature of the beliefs in question. TST meets every test that those other religions meet, and more.

The Philosophical Case

Beyond the legal arguments, there is a powerful philosophical case for recognizing modern Satanic groups. Religious liberty is not merely about protecting the religious—it is about protecting the principle that government should remain neutral in matters of conscience. When we permit the state to grant legal recognition to some faiths and withhold it from others based on theological content, we transform the state into an arbiter of orthodoxy. We invite the very establishment of religion that the First Amendment forbids.

Moreover, robust religious freedom requires the inclusion of unpopular religions. A right that protects only majority-approved beliefs is no right at all; it is merely a permission slip. The true test of a nation's commitment to religious liberty is how it treats the most unpopular, most misunderstood, most aesthetically challenging of its religious minorities. By that test, America's record is mixed at best—and recognition of TST is an opportunity to improve it.

Conclusion: Liberty for All, or Liberty for None

The Satanic Temple is a sincere, organized, doctrinally coherent religious movement that has won federal recognition, won legal victories, and demonstrated through its members' lives and conduct that its beliefs merit the same respect accorded to any other faith. To deny it legal recognition or equal protection would be to elevate prejudice over principle, to enshrine theological bias in our legal system, and to betray the foundational American commitment to religious pluralism.

Thomas Jefferson wrote that the First Amendment was designed to build "a wall of separation between church and state." That wall does not admit windows through which the state may peer to determine which religions are "real" and which are "fake." It is a wall of absolute neutrality, behind which every sincere believer—from the Methodist to the Muslim to the modern Satanic—is free to worship, or not worship, according to the dictates of their own conscience.

If we believe in religious freedom, we must believe in it for the religions we find strange, unsettling, or even frightening. Otherwise, we do not believe in religious freedom at all. We believe only in our own prerogative to decide which faiths deserve protection. That is not liberty. It is theocracy in a velvet glove.

The Satanic Temple, and all modern Satanic groups that meet the constitutional criteria for religious recognition, deserve full legal recognition and equal protection under the law. Anything less is a betrayal of the American founding—and an invitation to tyranny by any name.

When they offer to provide Satanic after-school programming where Christian programming is permitted, they are not mocking believers. They are insisting that public spaces belong equally to all of us, or to none of us through coercive endorsement.

This is the work of citizenship. This is what it looks like when a free people take their own principles seriously.

We will have proven that America, still, still, has the capacity to extend its circle of freedom one more time. We will have honored the dissidents, the heretics, and the freethinkers who built this country in the first place, often at tremendous cost.

The Conclusion

So I say to you: open the doors. Open the courts. Open the equal protection of our laws to modern Satanic groups as fully as you would open them to any other sincere religious community. Not because Satanism is fashionable. Not because we are called to endorse its theology. But because the alternative is a country where the government decides what counts as a faith — and that country is not the one our founders risked everything to create.

Religious freedom is not a menu from which the majority may pick and choose. It is a covenant. And a covenant, once broken, is broken for everyone.

Let us keep our covenant. Let us extend the blessings of liberty to all. And let us trust, in the words of the great tradition, that the light which shines for the comfortable will, if we let it, shine just as surely for the stranger at the gate.
